extracted.intended_audience: literary translators of Latin poetry (Horace), scholar-translators and advanced students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practical criteria for translating Horace's Satires, Epistles, and Art of Poetry into English verse — covering metre, style, fidelity, handling of local allusions, and editorial decisions about omission and modernization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre choice (heroic vs Hudibrastic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose an English metrical scheme to represent Horace's Latin hexameters — the author favors the English heroic (ten-syllable heroic couplet) over the Hudibrastic octosyllabic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: heroic couplet (as used by Cowper) can represent changes of mood and maintain terseness and ease; Hudibrastic octosyllabic, while historically used, tends in its colloquial form to become slipshod and unclassical. Consider the recognized metre of English satire; avoid using an English metrical distinction that has no Latin equivalent. Examples cited: Cowper as a model for heroic; Smart, Boscawen, Francis, Swift, Pope, and Cowper's use of the shorter form are discussed as precedents and counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of metrical treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not apply different English metres to different Horatian poems where no such distinction exists in the Latin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The translator argues against drawing a metrical line in English where none is drawn in Latin; inconsistent application (some poems in one metre, some in another) is objectionable where it can reasonably be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for idiomatic English (language of good society)
rubrics_metrics.description: Render Horace's persiflage and colloquial tone using the ordinary language of good society — conversation and familiar letter-writing — rather than artificially literary diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making the author vulgar or flat; seek an idiomatic prosaic ring. The translator adopted colloquial abbreviations and a conversational tone extensively, except where formality is required. Prefer conversational/familiar-letter idiom over 'the better sort of light literature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of persiflage and manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserve Horace's manner (persiflage, ease, terseness) rather than trying to translate isolated 'clever' lines literally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The charm of Horace depends on manner; a translator risks losing charm or individuality. Where Horace 'means to rise,' attempt to rise; for the greater part, aim to 'creep along the ground.' Beware triviality, pertness, and vulgarity; choose slips prudently when inevitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation principle (prioritize whole-sentence/paragraph effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate with the principle of compensation: accept losses in individual lines when necessary to recover overall effect in the sentence or paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge success by general effects and ultimate result rather than strict line-by-line fidelity. The important question is whether the combined English lines produce an effect comparable to the Latin; one may deliberately 'sharpen a point' or supply a turn that is implicit in Latin but would be insipid in English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity to spirit over literal word-for-word fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bear the Latin in mind but be prepared to depart from literal wording to preserve spirit, idiom, and overall effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator admits his version will be 'less close' than others; he studied commentators but took latitude where necessary. The choice is not between 'this line' and 'that line' but whether the English conforms to the requirements of the whole sentence/paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of epigram, pungency, and added turns
rubrics_metrics.description: When Latin epigrammatic or witty turns would read as flat in English, supply epigrammatic sharpness or pungency where appropriate to restore liveliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small additions to increase vivacity are acceptable as compensation for losses elsewhere. Cowper's remark is quoted: 'That is epigrammatic and witty in Latin which would be perfectly insipid in English; a translator ... find himself obliged to supply what is called the turn.' Use such additions cautiously and in service of the author's spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling local/temporary allusions (three approaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: For local, temporary, or cultural references, choose among three courses: (1) translate more or less verbally (risking unintelligibility), (2) generalize the specific, or (3) introduce a modern equivalent (imitator's licence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a mix of methods as advisable; use modern equivalents sparingly to avoid wantonly sacrificing the exposure of ancient life and thought. Examples: transforming a scarus into 'sardine' is permissible; avoid gross anachronisms like turning a Roman caena into an English dinner or saying 'the new Lord Mayor' for ancient contexts (Dryden-era excesses criticized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion of measures, sums, and minor particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapt monetary amounts, food items, and other minor particulars to English equivalents where it aids comprehension or metre, but avoid wholesale transformation of antiquities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator admits to sometimes converting sestertia into English sums roughly (e.g., 'so many hundreds' instead of exact conversion). Use discretion: do not pretend to distil Latin antiquities from the translation, but do not betray the antique spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission versus paraphrase policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit passages that are untranslatable, offensive, or unsuitable for modern readers rather than paraphrasing them awkwardly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator omitted two entire satires and several passages from others; where he did not translate, he generally remained silent rather than paraphrase. Some passages might have been translatable in earlier eras but are better left untranslated now.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model selection and selective borrowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a stylistic model (Cowper recommended for heroic couplet + ease/ terseness) and borrow selectively from other masters like Pope to gain grace, but avoid slavish imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cowper provides the right model for ease and terseness; Pope has terseness that is 'trimness and antithetical smartness' which may not suit Horace. Borrow grace from Pope occasionally, but avoid exposure to unequal comparison with predecessors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-literary or overly 'poetical' renderings
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from choosing English expressions that are poetical for their own sake when a prosaic idiom would better match Horace's tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a rendering presents itself that would be welcome as 'poetical' in another author, deliberately reject it in favor of something with an idiomatic prosaic ring, except where the original genuinely rises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of colloquial abbreviations and contractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ colloquial abbreviations in verse when appropriate to maintain spoken tone and idiomatic English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cowper proscribed colloquial abbreviations, but the translator adopted them freely through nearly the whole version except where formality required full forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience calibration (scholar vs general reader)
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance fidelity and readability according to the intended audience: a general reader may prefer a freer, more idiomatic translation, while the scholar may fault departures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator explicitly aims to give 'so much of my author as a well-judging reader would wish to dwell on in reading the original, and no more.' He accepts possible scholarly censure for liberties taken for the general reader's benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial ethics and provenance (acknowledging predecessors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of and acknowledge conscious debts to prior translators and commentators; avoid excessive consultation before producing your own independent rendering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator states he avoided consulting previous translations on a passage until he had translated it himself; conscious indebtedness is noted in the notes. Coincidences with predecessors may occur but need not be emphasized if they are incidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representing changes of mood within poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the English verse form can accommodate shifts of mood (light to grave and back) found in Horace's hexameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace's lightest Satires have something grave and the gravest have light passages; the heroic couplet, managed as Cowper does, is deemed adequate to represent these variations without imposing artificial metrical boundaries.
